name: Haudenosaunee
info: The Haudenosaunee, "those who build the longhouse", also called the Iroquois or Six Nations, are a confederacy of Iroquoian peoples of northeast North America, united under the Great Law of Peace and still governed by their Grand Council.

facts.homeland: south of the Great Lakes, in what is now New York State, from the Mohawk in the east to the Seneca in the west, with territory of over 75,000 square km in the 16th century; today seven reserves in Canada, among them the Six Nations of the Grand River, Akwesasne, Kahnawake and Kanesatake, and eleven reservations in the United States, in New York, Wisconsin and Oklahoma
facts.period: the League formed before European contact, likely between 1142 and 1660, by many scholars about 1450; the Beaver Wars from 1609; the Great Peace of Montreal of 1701; the Tuscarora joined in 1722; the American Revolution and the Sullivan Expedition of 1779; the fight for recognition at the League of Nations in 1923; living nations today
facts.known: the Great Law of Peace and the Grand Council of chiefs; the power of the Clan Mothers; the Hiawatha Belt and the Two Row Wampum; the longhouse; the Three Sisters of beans, maize and squash; the Thanksgiving Address; the Longhouse Religion of Handsome Lake; lacrosse
facts.sources: Haudenosaunee oral history of the Peacemaker, Hiawatha and Jigonhsasee, and the wampum belts; the writings of Samuel de Champlain from 1603 and other colonial records; Lewis Henry Morgan's studies in the 19th century; archaeological dating of the 125 villages of 1500 to 1700; the work of historians and anthropologists such as Richter, Dean Snow and Elisabeth Tooker

t: Haudenosaunee oral history tells that the Great Peacemaker, Hiawatha and Jigonhsasee united five warring nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, under the Great Law of Peace; the Tuscarora joined as the sixth nation in 1722.
Kinship is matrilineal, and the Clan Mothers choose the chiefs of the Grand Council and can remove a chief who fails his people.

For nearly 200 years the Haudenosaunee often held the balance of power between the French and British colonies, until the American Revolution split the Confederacy and cost it most of its lands in New York.
dyk: The Haudenosaunee government has issued its own passports since 1923, when it gave one to the Cayuga statesman Deskaheh to travel to the League of Nations.
ev: Many scholars date the forming of the Great League of Peace to about this time
The League begins the decades-long Beaver Wars against the French, the Wendat and other neighbours
The Haudenosaunee sign the Great Peace of Montreal with the French
The Tuscarora are accepted as the sixth nation of the Confederacy
The Sullivan Expedition destroys between 40 and 60 Haudenosaunee towns and villages
In a Treaty of Fort Stanwix the Haudenosaunee cede much of their homeland to the United States
Deskaheh petitions the League of Nations in Geneva on behalf of the Six Nations
A dispute over land at Oka, Quebec, leads to the Oka Crisis

sections.origins:
The Haudenosaunee League was established before European contact, when five Iroquoian peoples living south of the Great Lakes banded together into "The Great League of Peace". Many archaeologists and anthropologists date it to about 1450, while arguments have been made for dates as early as the solar eclipse of August 31, 1142; overall there is little agreement, and the range given runs from 1142 to 1660. From east to west the League joined the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca nations, each with its own Iroquoian language, territory and role.

Haudenosaunee spiritual history tells of dark times of terror and misery before the Confederacy, ended by the arrival of the Great Peacemaker, Dekanawida. With Hiawatha and Jigonhsasee, the Mother of Nations, whose home served as a kind of United Nations, he brought the Great Law of Peace to nations that were fighting and feuding with one another. Tradition holds that he proved himself the Creator's messenger by climbing a tall tree above a waterfall, having it cut down, and reappearing unharmed the next morning, and that he and Jigonhsasee turned the violent Hiawatha and Tadodaho to the message of peace.

The name Haudenosaunee means "people of the longhouse": a metaphorical longhouse reaching from the Mohawk, "Keepers of the Eastern Door", to the Seneca, "Keepers of the Western Door". Iroquois, the old exonym, is of obscure and debated origin and first appears in Samuel de Champlain's writings of 1603.
sections.society:
Within each of the Six Nations people belong to matrilineal clans, today from three to eight in a nation, with nine clan names in all. Children belong to their mother's clan and take their status from it, and her brothers are their important teachers. Marrying within one's matrilineal clan is regarded as incest. A young couple traditionally lived in the longhouse of the wife's family, women held the dwellings and farmed land, and a woman kept her own property after marriage and could ask an unsatisfactory husband to leave.

The Haudenosaunee have historically followed a matriarchal system in which men and women had separate roles and both held real power. No person owns land, but the Creator is believed to have appointed women as its stewards. The Clan Mothers appoint the leaders and can strip a corrupt or unheeding chief of his office, a process called "dehorning", in which the deer antlers of leadership were taken from his headgear. Women held the power to veto treaties or declarations of war, met in their own councils and often proposed legislation. In 1855 Minnie Myrtle observed that no treaty was binding unless ratified by 75% of the men and 75% of the mothers of the nation.

The Grand Council of the Six Nations is an assembly of 56 chiefs whose offices are hereditary within their clans: 14 Onondaga, 10 Cayuga, 9 Oneida, 9 Mohawk, 8 Seneca and 6 Tuscarora. Lewis Henry Morgan read it as a central government; Richter argues that decisions are made locally, by community consensus. Each clan keeps a group of personal names, tracked by the clan mother.
sections.beliefs:
The Haudenosaunee believed in many deities, among them the Creator or Great Spirit, the Thunderer and the Three Sisters, the spirits of beans, maize and squash. Orenda is the proposed Iroquoian name for the spiritual force that flows through people and all things. Accounts of creation differ. One tells of Sky Woman, Aientsik, whose daughter Tekawerahkwa bore twins: Okwiraseh, who made "all that is pure and beautiful", and Tawiskaron, who made vicious animals and rapids and was confined to the dark areas of the world. Other scholars present the twins as the Creator and his brother Flint.

Dreams play a significant role, revealing a person's desires, and prayers are sent to the spirits by burning tobacco. Condolence ceremonies are held for the dead, above all for a chief; the soul is thought to journey for a year to the sky world, after which a feast celebrates its arrival. Faithkeepers, men and women appointed by the elders, conduct ceremonies. The Thanksgiving Address, recited at the start of school days and at gatherings, gives thanks in 17 sections, from the people and the Earth Mother to the Creator. Festivals follow the seasons and the farming year: Maple, Planting, Strawberry, Green Maize, Harvest and the Mid-winter festival that opens the new year. Fraternal medicine societies, of which the False Face Society is the best known, conduct healing rituals.

After European arrival some Haudenosaunee became Christians, among them Kateri Tekakwitha, the first Native American saint. In the late 18th century the Seneca chief Handsome Lake founded a new religion joining Quaker beliefs to Iroquoian tradition, the Gaihwi꞉io or Longhouse Religion; by the 1960s at least 50% of Haudenosaunee followed it.
sections.arts:
Haudenosaunee art includes wood carving, pottery, quillwork, beadwork, basketry, husk work, silverwork, clothing, jewellery and wampum. Older works carried animal, human and geometric imagery on wood, bowls, pottery and clay pipes, while later beadwork often used floral designs. In the 19th century the Haudenosaunee Realist School brought Haudenosaunee subjects and stories into watercolour, and artists of the 20th and 21st centuries have worked in painting, sculpture, video and installation. The Seneca embroiderer and beadworker Caroline G. Parker joined Haudenosaunee and Victorian styles, with a lasting influence on Seneca and Tuscarora fashion.

Wampum, beads of purple and white mollusc shell on threads of elm bark, was made chiefly into belts, which tradition says Hiawatha invented to console chiefs and clan mothers who had lost kin to war. The belts serve in the Condolence Ceremony, at the raising of new chiefs and in treaty making. The Hiawatha Belt, the national belt shown on the Confederacy's flag, has four squares and a tree, the eastern white pine that stands for the Tree of Peace and for the Onondaga, the keepers of peace. The Two Row Wampum shows a canoe and a sailboat moving side by side without crossing each other's course.

Men's traditional dress included moccasins, leggings, short kilts and the feathered gustoweh cap, and the Mohawk gave their name to a hairstyle. From the 18th century red and blue European cloth, decorated with beadwork, quillwork and ribbons, became standard. Lacrosse has a long history among the Haudenosaunee, who field their own national teams.
sections.exchange:
Contact with Europeans began with the Dutch at Fort Nassau, with whom the Haudenosaunee soon traded; their oral tradition ties this meeting to the Two Row Wampum Treaty of coexistence and non-interference. By the 1640s the Mohawk, through their hold on the Fort Orange (Albany) market, were selling the Dutch thousands of furs a year. Muskets from the fur trade fed the Beaver Wars from 1609, in which the League fought the French and their Wendat allies and defeated and assimilated most of the Wendat (1649), Petun (1650), Neutral Nation (1651), Erie (1657) and Susquehannock (1680). From the mid-1670s they were allied with the English in the Covenant Chain, and in 1701 they made the Great Peace of Montreal with the French.

The Haudenosaunee backed the British in the French and Indian War, and the Royal Proclamation of 1763 forbade white settlement beyond the Appalachians, an order the colonists largely ignored. In the American Revolution League unity broke down: the Oneida and Tuscarora supported the colonists, the others the British. In 1779 the Sullivan Expedition destroyed between 40 and 60 towns and villages in a scorched earth operation, and by one estimate 4,500 died in its aftermath. The 1783 Treaty of Paris ceded Haudenosaunee land in New York without provision for them, and the treaties of Fort Stanwix (1784) and Canandaigua (1794) took much of the rest.

Epidemics struck as well: Jones estimates the population at 20,000 in 1620–1634 and at 8,000 in 1634 to 1660, not counting the thousands adopted.
sections.legacy:
After the Revolution many Haudenosaunee moved to Canada, where the Crown gave land at the Grand River, and those in New York were confined mostly to reservations. In the 20th century they defended their sovereignty. The Six Nations council at Brantford saw itself as allied directly to the Crown through the Covenant Chain, and in 1923 Deskaheh carried its petition to the League of Nations in Geneva; it was blocked, and in 1924 Canada replaced the traditional chiefs' council with one elected under the Indian Act. The Grand Council declared war on Germany in 1917 and again in 1942. In the United States the nations resisted termination in the 1950s and 1960s, and no New York tribe was terminated, though the Kinzua Dam dislocated about 500 Seneca. In 1990 a dispute over land at Oka, Quebec, led to the Oka Crisis.

In 2010 more than 45,000 enrolled Six Nations people lived in Canada and over 81,000 in the United States, with sovereignty over seven reserves in Canada and eleven reservations in the United States. The Six Nations of the Grand River is the largest First Nations reserve in Canada, and the Grand Council still exists. In the 2020 U.S. census 113,814 people identified as Haudenosaunee.

The status of Haudenosaunee women influenced the early American feminist movement around the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848. Whether their government influenced the U.S. Constitution is disputed: Congress recognised such an influence in 1988, while Jack N. Rakove, Dean Snow and Elisabeth Tooker find little or no evidence that the framers borrowed from it.

summary: The Haudenosaunee are a confederacy of Iroquoian nations who, by their own history, were united by the Great Peacemaker under the Great Law of Peace. Matrilineal clans and powerful Clan Mothers shape their government. A great power between the French and British for nearly two centuries, they lost most of their lands after the American Revolution but keep their Grand Council, nations and reserves today.
references: Morgan, Lewis H. (1870). Systems of Consanguinity and Affinity of the Human Family
